summary: Piroxicam is a long-acting oxicam NSAID used for the signs and symptoms of osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis. Its very long half-life allows once-daily dosing but increases the risk of cumulative toxicity. It carries a boxed warning for serious cardiovascular thrombotic and gastrointestinal bleeding events.
indications: Relief of the signs and symptoms of osteoarthritis (OA)
Relief of the signs and symptoms of rheumatoid arthritis (RA)

dosage.t: Daily dose may be divided if desired; assess response at 2 weeks (steady state in 7-12 days)
dosage.n: Use lowest effective dose for shortest duration

dosage.t: Daily dose may be divided if desired; therapeutic response increases progressively over several weeks
dosage.n: Use lowest effective dose for shortest duration

admin: Take by mouth once daily, preferably with food to reduce GI upset
Do not assess therapeutic effect before about 2 weeks because steady-state levels are reached only after 7-12 days
Antacids (aluminum hydroxide +/- magnesium hydroxide) do not affect plasma levels
Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration consistent with treatment goals
moa: Like other NSAIDs, piroxicam inhibits cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2), reducing prostaglandin synthesis. Lower peripheral prostaglandin levels diminish the sensitization of afferent nerves and inflammatory mediation, producing analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and antipyretic effects.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to piroxicam (including anaphylaxis and serious skin reactions) or any component
History of asthma, urticaria, or other allergic-type reaction after aspirin or other NSAIDs
Use in the setting of coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery
relative: Severe heart failure (avoid unless benefit outweighs risk)
Advanced renal disease (avoid unless benefit outweighs risk)
History of peptic ulcer disease or GI bleeding
monitor: Cardiovascular thrombotic events (MI, stroke) - risk may begin early and rise with duration
Serious GI bleeding, ulceration, and perforation, especially in elderly
Hepatotoxicity - discontinue if liver tests worsen or signs of liver disease appear
Renal function in renal/hepatic impairment, heart failure, dehydration, or hypovolemia

preg: Use of NSAIDs in the third trimester increases the risk of premature closure of the fetal ductus arteriosus; avoid starting at 30 weeks gestation. First- and second-trimester data are inconclusive. NSAIDs can also cause reversible infertility, so consider withdrawal in women having difficulty conceiving.
lact: Piroxicam passes into human milk at roughly 1% to 3% of maternal plasma concentration without accumulation; weigh benefits against potential infant risk and generally avoid during breastfeeding.
renal: Monitor renal function in patients with renal impairment, heart failure, dehydration, or hypovolemia. Avoid use in advanced renal disease unless expected benefits outweigh the risk of worsening renal function.
hepatic: Use with caution; monitor liver tests and inform patients of signs of hepatotoxicity. Discontinue if abnormal liver tests persist or worsen or if clinical liver disease develops.

major: Anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin) - synergistic, increased risk of serious bleeding
Aspirin - increased GI bleeding; not recommended together and piroxicam does not replace cardioprotective aspirin
SSRIs/SNRIs - increased bleeding risk via platelet serotonin effects
moderate: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and beta-blockers - reduced antihypertensive effect; risk of acute renal failure in elderly/volume-depleted/renally impaired patients
Diuretics - reduced natriuretic effect and added renal risk
Other NSAIDs - additive GI and renal toxicity
minor: Antacids (aluminum/magnesium hydroxide) - no clinically significant effect on piroxicam levels
interactions.food: May be taken with food, which slightly delays but does not reduce the extent of absorption.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid; alcohol adds to the risk of GI bleeding and ulceration.
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor hemoglobin/hematocrit, renal function, liver tests, and blood pressure during therapy.

emergency: Anaphylactic reaction (difficulty breathing, facial or throat swelling)
Serious skin reactions (e.g., SJS/TEN) - stop at first rash or hypersensitivity sign
Symptoms of MI or stroke (chest pain, breathlessness, weakness, slurred speech)

monitoring: Signs and symptoms of GI bleeding and cardiovascular events
counsel: Take once daily with food; do not exceed the prescribed dose
Report chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness, or slurred speech immediately (cardiovascular events)
Report black/bloody stools, vomiting blood, or epigastric pain (GI bleeding)
Watch for jaundice, dark urine, nausea, fatigue, or right upper-quadrant pain (liver injury) and stop the drug
Seek emergency care for trouble breathing or facial/throat swelling, or any new rash
Avoid alcohol and concurrent aspirin or other NSAIDs unless directed
Inform clinician if pregnant, especially after 30 weeks, or if planning pregnancy
pearls: Very long half-life (~50 hours) gives once-daily dosing but means steady state and toxicity build over 7-12 days - assess response only after about 2 weeks
99% protein-bound, so dialysis and forced diuresis are of little use in overdose
Contraindicated around CABG surgery and in aspirin/NSAID-allergic patients
Higher GI and CV risk in the elderly - use the lowest dose for the shortest time
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed one and resume the regular once-daily schedule. Do not double the dose.
overdose: Acute overdose usually causes lethargy, drowsiness, nausea, vomiting, and epigastric pain and is generally reversible with supportive care; GI bleeding, hypertension, acute renal failure, respiratory depression, and coma are rare. There is no specific antidote. Manage symptomatically; consider emesis and/or activated charcoal (60-100 g in adults; 1-2 g/kg in children) within 4 hours of ingestion or with large overdose. High protein binding makes forced diuresis, urine alkalinization, hemodialysis, and hemoperfusion of limited value. Contact a poison control center (1-800-222-1222).
